title: Can you overdose on Suboxone®? Symptoms, risks, and what to do
summary: Can you overdose on Suboxone (buprenorphine/naloxone)? Learn why the risk is low, what raises it, overdose signs, and what to do in an emergency.
body_markdown:
Yes, like any opioid medication, Suboxone can cause an overdose, but it’s far less likely than with heroin, fentanyl, or other full opioids. Buprenorphine has a “ceiling effect”: past a certain dose, taking more doesn’t increase its effect on your breathing. Most Suboxone overdoses, rare as they are, involve mixing it with alcohol or sedatives, taking it without opioid tolerance, or even a child swallowing it by accident.


For people with opioid use disorder, the bigger risk is going without treatment. Staying on Suboxone is linked to a much lower risk of overdose. Like any medication, it has risks, and your care team’s job is to help you manage them so treatment can do its job.


## Key takeaways


- **Treatment lowers overdose risk dramatically.** Buprenorphine or methadone is linked to a 76% lower risk of overdose at three months compared with no treatment.
- **Overdosing on Suboxone alone is rare.** In a CDC and NIDA study of 74,474 opioid overdose deaths, buprenorphine was involved in 2.6% — and nearly 93% of those deaths also involved at least one other drug.
- **The ceiling effect is why.** Buprenorphine's effect on breathing levels off at higher doses, which is a big part of what makes it safer than full opioids.
- **The real risks are mixing and tolerance.** Danger comes from combining Suboxone with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other sedatives — and from people without opioid tolerance taking it, including children.
- **The naloxone in Suboxone isn't overdose protection.** When the film dissolves in your mouth, the naloxone does little; it's there to discourage injecting the medication.
- **If you suspect an overdose, call 911 and give naloxone (Narcan).** A buprenorphine overdose may need more than one dose.


[Suboxone®](https://ophelia.com/suboxone) ([important safety information](https://ophelia.com/suboxone-safety) ) is a brand--name FDA-approved prescription medication (generic: buprenorphine/naloxone) used in medication-assisted treatment (MAT) for opioid use disorder (OUD).


As a partial[opioid agonist](https://ophelia.com/glossary/agonist) , it does activate opioid receptors but much less so than heroin or fentanyl, which are both full opioids. It’s for this reason that[buprenorphine](https://ophelia.com/blog/what-is-buprenorphine) eases withdrawal and cravings without producing a strong opioid high in people who already have opioid tolerance.


Because it’s often taken long-term, sometimes for years, some may naturally have questions about the risk of overdose on a[Suboxone treatment program](https://ophelia.com/suboxone-doctors) . Here’s what you need to know.


## **How likely is a Suboxone overdose?**


You are far less likely to overdose on Suboxone than on other opioids. The reason? In people who take it regularly, buprenorphine’s ceiling effect means higher doses don’t keep slowing breathing the way full opioids do. However, people who are not taking Suboxone regularly (and are therefore not tolerant) can become very sedated with slowed breathing after taking Suboxone. This is particularly true for children who accidentally take the medication.


The research is reassuring. A CDC and NIDA analysis of 74,474 opioid-involved overdose deaths between July 2019 and June 2021 found that buprenorphine was involved in 2.6% of them, and 92.7% of those deaths also involved at least one other drug. Buprenorphine-involved deaths were also less likely than other opioid deaths to involve illicit fentanyl.


For people with opioid use disorder, Suboxone lowers the overall risk of overdose. In a study of more than 40,000 people, treatment with buprenorphine or methadone was linked to a 76% lower risk of overdose at three months and a 59% lower risk at 12 months, compared with no treatment.


## **Can you overdose on Suboxone if it contains naloxone?**


Yes. The naloxone in Suboxone doesn’t protect you from an overdose. When the film dissolves under your tongue or inside your cheek, only a small amount of naloxone reaches your bloodstream, so it has no meaningful effect. It’s added to discourage misuse, like injecting Suboxone: if someone dependent on opioids like heroin or fentanyl injects Suboxone, the naloxone is likely to set off sudden withdrawal.


Naloxone doesn’t cause an overdose either. The risk comes from buprenorphine, so the same precautions apply to generic buprenorphine/naloxone films and tablets and to[buprenorphine-only medication](https://ophelia.com/treatment-online-subutex) (once sold under the brand name Subutex).


## **How to take Suboxone safely**


Most people who take Suboxone as prescribed never have an overdose. These are the situations that make an overdose more likely.


### **Avoid mixing Suboxone with alcohol and sedatives**


This is the most common factor in Suboxone-related overdoses. Benzodiazepines (such as Xanax or Klonopin), alcohol, sleep medications, gabapentin or pregabalin, muscle relaxants, and other opioids all slow down your central nervous system. Combined with buprenorphine, they can slow breathing past the point where the ceiling effect protects you. In the CDC and NIDA study, 36.9% of buprenorphine-involved overdose deaths also involved benzodiazepines. The danger is even greater when Suboxone is misused by injection, which is different from prescribed[Sublocade injections](https://ophelia.com/sublocade-treatment) .


Taking a prescribed sedative doesn’t automatically rule out Suboxone. FDA labeling states that treatment shouldn’t be denied for this reason, since untreated opioid use disorder carries serious risks of its own. Tell your care team about everything you take so they can plan around it. Learn more about[Suboxone drug interactions](https://ophelia.com/blog/suboxone-drug-interactions) .


### **Don’t share your medication**


Your dose is prescribed for you. Someone who doesn’t use opioids, or hasn’t in a while, may have little or no opioid tolerance, so even a small amount can slow their breathing dangerously. That’s why Suboxone should never be shared.


### **Keep Suboxone away from children**


The most important safety step at home is keeping Suboxone away from children. Even one film can cause severe, possibly fatal, breathing problems in a child, and because buprenorphine is long-acting, the effects can last for hours. Store Suboxone in a locked place out of sight and reach, and dispose of unused films safely. If a child may have swallowed or chewed Suboxone, call 911 right away, even if they seem fine. For questions, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.


### **Share your full medication list with your care team**


Some medications raise buprenorphine levels in the body and can increase sedation, including certain antibiotics (such as erythromycin), antifungals (such as ketoconazole), and some HIV medications. People with lung conditions like COPD, moderate to severe liver problems, or who are 65 or older may also need closer monitoring. Your clinician reviews your health history and medications before prescribing and adjusts your plan if anything changes.


### **Don’t stop treatment suddenly**


Stopping Suboxone too soon, or all at once, can bring back withdrawal and cravings and lead to a return to opioid use. Your tolerance to other opioids drops during treatment, so going back to a previous amount of heroin, fentanyl, or pills can cause an overdose.[One study](https://ophelia.com/research/opioid-following-discontinuation-of-long-term-buprenorphine-treatment) found that about 1 in 20 people needed medical care for an opioid overdose in the six months after stopping buprenorphine, even after 6-18 months of treatment.


That said, many people successfully taper off Suboxone after a long period of maintenance with it. The key is to work with your healthcare provider to ensure that you are[tapering off](https://ophelia.com/glossary/tapering) the medication at the right pace, that you have the tools to deal with any unpleasant side effects and withdrawal symptoms that may arise, and that you have a good plan for how to stay protected against a return to opioid use after discontinuing Suboxone. The Ophelia team can help you prepare for safely stopping the medication, which includes peer and therapy support, and possibly a period of treatment with another medication such as naltrexone. There’s no set end date for Suboxone treatment. Many people do best staying on it long term, and the decision to stop is one you make together with your clinician.


## **Symptoms of a Suboxone overdose**


While the risks are low, it is important to be aware of the symptoms of a Suboxone overdose, which are similar to those of other opioid overdoses:


- Extreme sleepiness or being hard to wake up
- Slow, shallow, or stopped breathing
- Pinpoint (very small) pupils
- Blue or gray lips or fingertips
- Gurgling or snoring sounds
- Low blood pressure, dizziness, or fainting
- A limp body or not responding


Because buprenorphine stays in the body for a long time, symptoms can last for hours and can come back after naloxone wears off. Treat any suspected overdose as a medical emergency, even if the person seems to improve.


## **What to do if you think someone overdosed on Suboxone**


1. **Call 911.** Tell the dispatcher the person may have taken buprenorphine, along with any other substances you know about.
2. **Give naloxone (Narcan) if you have it.** Buprenorphine binds tightly to opioid receptors, so it may take a higher dose or more than one dose of naloxone to work. If there’s no response after two to three minutes, give another dose.
3. **Support their breathing.** If you’re trained, give rescue breaths. If they’re breathing, roll them onto their side so they don’t choke.
4. **Stay with them until help arrives.** Naloxone wears off before buprenorphine does, so symptoms can return. Anyone who needs naloxone for a Suboxone overdose should get medical care.


Naloxone nasal spray is available without a prescription at most pharmacies.

## **Frequently asked questions about Suboxone overdose**


### **How much Suboxone does it take to overdose?**


There’s no set amount. It depends on your opioid tolerance, your health, and what else is in your system. A dose that’s routine for one person can be dangerous for someone without tolerance, and deaths have been reported after a single 2 mg dose in people with no tolerance. Take only what your clinician prescribes, and never share your medication.


### **What happens if I take more Suboxone than prescribed?**


Yes, you can take too much Suboxone. What happens if you take too much depends on your dose, opioid tolerance, and other substances you’ve taken. Side effects of too much Suboxone can include marked drowsiness, dizziness, low blood pressure, and dangerously slow breathing.


If you take more than prescribed, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away for guidance. If someone is hard to wake or breathing slowly, call 911 and give naloxone if available. Let your clinician know so they can review your dosing plan.


### **Can Suboxone kill you?**


It’s rare. When Suboxone is taken as prescribed, serious overdose is uncommon, and most deaths involving buprenorphine also involve other drugs like benzodiazepines or alcohol. For people with opioid use disorder, the greater danger is not being in treatment: staying on Suboxone lowers the overall risk of overdose.


### **Can you overdose on Suboxone if you also use fentanyl?**


Yes. At a steady dose, buprenorphine binds tightly to opioid receptors and can blunt the effects of other opioids, including[fentanyl](https://ophelia.com/fentanyl-addiction-treatment) . That protection depends on your dose and isn’t guaranteed, and fentanyl’s strength makes any use risky. If you’ve used fentanyl or other opioids while on Suboxone, tell your care team so they can adjust your plan.


### **Is feeling sick after my first dose a sign of overdose?**


Usually not. Feeling suddenly worse after a first dose is more often[precipitated withdrawal](https://ophelia.com/blog/what-is-precipitated-withdrawal) , which happens when Suboxone is taken while other opioids are still active in your system. It causes intense withdrawal symptoms, so contact your care team right away. Extreme sleepiness or slow breathing, on the other hand, are signs of overdose and need emergency care.


### **Should I keep naloxone at home if I take Suboxone?**


Yes. FDA labeling recommends that people taking Suboxone have access to an overdose reversal medication like naloxone, especially if children or other people in the home could be exposed. Naloxone nasal spray is sold without a prescription at most pharmacies. Make sure the people you live with know where it is and how to use it.
